item.title: What I'd Tell My Inner Child Now
item.description:
Therapy

What I'd Tell My Inner Child Now

Personal Perspective: With some AI image help, we can speak to our six-year-old selves.

Posted August 11, 2026

Key points
  • AI-generated video is proving to be a new tool for the "auxiliary ego" work at psychodrama's core.
  • Animating an old childhood photo with AI created a genuine psychodrama-style "encounter" with myself.
  • Speaking to my inner child yielded honest counsel on worry, love, friendship, and resilience.
AI generated: The author at six— and now, sitting down beside him.
Source: AI-generated image; Comapps LLC, 2026

There's an old photograph that opens my memoir, Confessions of a Former Child: A Therapist's Memoir. In it, I'm maybe six years old, dressed head to toe in cowboy gear—hat, chaps, bandanna, the whole sheriff-gonna-clean-up-Dodge kit—looking at the world like I already had a few things figured out. This is how I dressed on Saturday mornings back then.

Earlier this week, my wife, Andrea, on a whim, fed that photograph into an AI video tool (Comapps LLC., 2026) and asked it to imagine something that never could have happened: Me, as I am now—white-bearded, with a grandpa's worth of stories in my pocket—sitting down next to that boy on a bench. Then hugging him.

I wasn't prepared for what this did to me.

I've spent a career studying how psychodrama can facilitate hope, gratitude, and love. I know, intellectually, that "inner child work" is a real clinical tool, and that psychodrama founder J.L. Moreno (1987) built an entire method around exactly this kind of encounter—using an empty chair or a fellow group member as an auxiliary ego to stand in for a piece of the self that needs to be met, not managed.

What I wasn't ready for was how differently it lands when the auxiliary ego isn't a stranger playing a role, or an empty chair you have to imagine filling—when it's actually you. The very crease of that six-year-old's mouth, caught by a photographer in 1957, had now been animated into looking up at me the way he used to look up at the sky.

When I first saw the video, I knew psychodrama had entered a new era. I know that feeling of watching and participating in an enactment, and the transformation possible in one. As the video replayed, the drama that unfolded was as rich as any I'd taken part in or directed in real time. My inner child was alive, and he needed a hug. He was also wondering what the future would be like.

I sat with my little six-year-old cowboy for a while, let the video run, and told him some things I thought he'd like to know.

The first thing I explained was that, although he very much wanted to be a cowboy, he was never actually going to shoot a gun. That yes, he was going to be a peacemaker, but he'd use words and chairs as his tools rather than pistols.

I told him he'd be worried about a million things that would never happen. That nearly everything he was so carefully planning wasn't going to work out the way he thought—that life, for him, would mostly be the experience of aiming at one thing and getting surprised into another.

I told him that even in the moments he didn't feel loved, the plain fact that he was alive, conscious, and breathing was evidence enough. Something in the universe had gone to a great deal of trouble to love him into being.

I told him there would be scary moments—real ones, ones he couldn't see coming—and that these terrible times would turn out to be teachers in disguise, delivering exactly the lesson he needed, at a price he wouldn't have volunteered to pay.

I told him he'd get blindsided, unbelievably sad and confused, even to the point of needing therapy—and that would be one of the greatest gifts he'd ever receive.

I told him to keep a beginner's mind. To stay curious the way six-year-olds are curious, before the world convinces you that sounding certain is more impressive than being in a state of wonder. Not to get too serious, or too stuck on any one thing. That a flexible mindset is the best thing he could cultivate.

I told him to be sweet and generous every chance he got, because that sweetness would return to him a thousandfold. That he'd cry harder than he could imagine, and laugh twice as hard, and both would surprise him. That's how the universe gets his attention—the good surprises and the bad ones alike.

I told him to make friends and keep them, because in the end they're how he'll be known. That big parties and mountains of friends are nice early on, but a quiet dinner with your besties gets so much better with time.

I reminded him that although everything wasn't okay for him as a child, he'd get a chance to make it right when he became a father himself—that his parents did the best they could with what they had, and that the empty feelings and disappointments would become the raw material for becoming a better parent than they were.

I told him to take care of the one body he's got, because it's the only one he's getting. Watch what you eat, watch what you drink, and yes—wash your hands before you eat and brush your teeth. (Some wisdom just refuses to be profound.)

I told him he'd become a parent, and then a grandparent, and one day look into his own eyes again in the face of a grandchild—and that when that miracle happened, there'd be so much he'd want to share it would feel like bursting at the seams.

I told him to read, to pray, to meditate—not because those things are magic tricks that get you what you want, but because they're ways of remembering you didn't create yourself. That the fastest way out of a dark mood is almost always to go help somebody else out of theirs.

I told him his thoughts were the most powerful entities in the universe—not because they control what happens to him, but because they control how he receives what happens to him. It was never really about the events. It was about what he'd decide the events meant.

I told him that when he found a love that felt singular and alive and impossible to fake, to make it the priority of his life, above everything else. That the whole arc of his life was a long walk from fear to love, and whatever the problem or the question, the answer would always include love.

And last, I told him this: that a lot of people would betray him and disappoint him, and a lot more would surprise and delight him in ways he couldn't have scripted—and that none of it, none of the wreckage and none of the grace, would ever define him. Each encounter would simply be another chance for him to be revealed.

Then he hugged me, and we said goodbye for now.

item.title: Why We Never Finish Discovering the People We Love
item.description:
Relationships

Why We Never Finish Discovering the People We Love

What good relationships help us see.

Posted August 11, 2026

Key points
  • What once worked can stop working when we mistake a habit for the principle behind it.
  • When a relationship struggles, one useful question is: What is this relationship for?
  • Conflict reveals a relationship's character by showing whether we seek understanding or certainty.
  • Discernment is refined perception: the capacity to see more than our first interpretation allowed.

Executive coach Marshall Goldsmith’s What Got You Here Won’t Get You There (2007) is a rare title that feels self-evident. You understand its insight before you’ve read the first page.

SCENE:

A caring manager runs a small office. Every Friday, he calls the neighborhood donut shop. The ritual becomes part of the office culture. People look forward to it. His team feels appreciated. His boss notices the enthusiasm he’s building. Before long, the manager is promoted to a global role.

Friday morning arrives.

Manager: “Hey, Big T.”

Tony: “Morning, my friend. The usual mixed dozen for Donut Friday?”

Manager: “Actually…I got promoted.”

Tony: “Congratulations!”

Manager: “Thanks. I have absolutely no idea how to manage fifteen thousand people.”

Tony: “Hey, just stick with what you know.”

(Long pause.)

Manager: “You’re right. I need fifteen thousand donuts.”

The example is absurd, but the problem isn’t uncommon. People can succeed without clearly grasping why. And it crosses domains. Enter the athlete, who knows where the answer lies.

When a hitter suddenly goes 0-for-27, he knows something that got him here isn’t getting him there anymore. Modern baseball technology can detect tiny changes in bat speed and swing path, but the search for a way forward returns to the fundamentals.

What Got Us Here

Goldsmith’s title gives us the warning. Did we examine what got us here, or did we simply get habituated to what seemed successful? The “if it ain't broke, don’t fix it” mentality. Before long, you’re on autopilot, thinking you’re still flying the plane.

The hitter points us back to fundamentals. Another route begins with one of philosophy’s oldest questions. What is this for? Aristotle made that question central to his thinking. Before asking how to do something well, he wanted to know what it was for. Clarifying the purpose, the telos, comes first.

Thus, we can get beneath a successful practice by asking two deceptively simple questions. What is fundamental here? What is this for?

What is leadership for? What is fundamental to good leadership? Once we start asking, the questions multiply:

  • What is dating for?
  • What is an apology for?
  • What is an argument for?
  • And, perhaps surprisingly, what is a donut for?

They sound obvious until we realize how often we take the answers for granted. Relationships can slump too.

A partner who has spent years showing love by providing may respond to emotional distance by becoming even more distant in order to provide more. What once brought two people closer may no longer do so as they and their circumstances change. Before we diagnose poor communication, incompatible styles, or bad habits, we might return to our two questions. What is a good relationship for? What are its fundamentals?

Learning to See More

Those questions only help if we can tolerate not answering them too quickly. It can be anxiety-provoking to realize how much may depend on getting them right. We may rush to judgment before we have seen enough. Patience, please.

Psychologist Michel Dugas and colleagues (2026) describe research on intolerance of uncertainty. When discomfort with not knowing makes us close the question too soon, we naturally strip away depth and nuance before they’ve had a chance to emerge. That’s premature closure.

As a professor, coach, actor, and director, I know this problem too. Giving an actor a line reading, “Say it this way,” forecloses deeper exploration before the actor has discovered what the moment holds.

If we can slow down and resist the rush to judgment, even as new, potentially confusing evidence pours in, we begin to develop a new kind of power: the ability to tolerate ambiguity. We now have greater capacity for discovery.

The French omelette remains one of the culinary world’s classic tests of mastery. Its simplicity leaves nowhere to hide.
Source: Dietmar Rauscher/iStock

So let’s refine our gaze and turn it to something seemingly simple: the French omelette.

Enter Jacques Pépin.

The legendary chef, author of La Technique, once said that if he had to judge another professional, he would ask them to make an omelette. Every detail matters: heat control, the shake, the roll, the baveuse center. Tiny bubbles? Overwhisked. Chef Thomas Keller credits Pépin with teaching him that “mastery begins with the fundamentals.” But mastery does something else. It changes what we can see. Expertise is not merely knowing more. It is seeing more. Discernment is refined perception.

Chefs have a phrase for preparing the conditions of excellence: mise en place, everything in its place. Ingredients are chopped, measured, and ready before cooking begins. Long before the first pan is heated, the work has begun.

Parenting is a kind of mise en place: preparing a child’s fundamental capacities for judgment, perception, and interpretation before either parent or child can know what life will ask of them.

The People We Think We Know

I remember an argument with my father when I was in high school. I don’t remember what started it, only one exchange:

Dad: “What do you do for me?”

Me at 15: “I’m in high school.”

I hadn’t found a smaller answer. I’d found the fundamental one. Later, he came back and apologized. I was surprised and relieved. At the time, I figured he’d heard my point and conceded. That memory stayed with me. I guess I wasn’t finished with it. I guess now is later.

With time, the same moment can reveal details we weren’t equipped to see before. Today, I can recognize something that escaped me then. There was probably more happening in that room than I knew. I don’t know exactly what my father was carrying, and I no longer need to. That didn’t excuse the hurt, nor erase his apology. What I understood at 15 remained true. It simply wasn’t everything that was true. I was no longer listening with the ears of a teenager.

Memory isn’t dead weight. Sometimes our earlier selves leave placeholders, archiving moments we can’t fully grasp yet. The child holds the place until the mature adult arrives to see what else was there.

If time can widen our view of an old argument, discernment asks whether we can make a little room for that wider view while we’re still having one.

We often screen potential partners for attractiveness and charm. Maybe we should pay more attention to how they reveal themselves through conflict. The next time you find yourself in an argument, notice how quickly your mind reaches certainty. How quickly you decide what the other person meant and what kind of person they must be. That is precisely the moment to resist premature closure.

Ask the fundamental question: What are we fighting for? If the answer is domination, the conversation is already lost. If the answer is understanding, stay with it longer. Allow the moment to reveal more than your first interpretation permitted. Scholars call this coalescent argumentation: uncovering shared values to transform disagreement into greater clarity. In a good relationship, it can alchemize negativity into closeness.

As I write this final paragraph, I ask Aristotle’s question one last time: What is this for?

Perhaps it's this: to never finish discovering the people we love. And that is a good thing because to love someone is to make room for who they are becoming. Goldsmith was right that what got us here won’t get us there, but that is simply what a dynamic life looks like.

We can stay curious about the person before us and honor the child who held the place until we were ready to see.

item.title: What Are Google Doodles and Why Do They Matter?
item.description:
Sexual Orientation

What Are Google Doodles and Why Do They Matter?

The importance of queer representation in Google Doodles.

Posted August 11, 2026

Key points
  • Doodles expose many topics to a wide variety of audiences and encourage exploration of diverse themes.
  • Of the 5,000+ Doodles, only about half a percent have featured LGBTQ-related content.
  • Positive queer media content is related to positive mental health among LGBTQ youth and reduces prejudice.

Have you ever wondered about the fun graphics that show up on Google’s search engine home page? Known as “Doodles,” these illustrations and animations are often artistic interpretations of the word “Google” that are both significant artifacts of collective memory and communicatory visual aids that highlight important people and events (Britten, 2020). Beyond this, Doodles have the unique ability to cross a wide variety of audiences, potentially encouraging engagement with themes, topics, and ideas beyond their typical scope of inquiry.

Since 1998, more than 5,000 Doodles have been created, mostly by a team of in-house artists (called "Doodlers"), though they sometimes partner with guest artists (The Story and Evolution of Doodles, Google Doodles, n.d.). However, of those 5,000+ Doodles, only about half a percent have featured LGBTQ-related content, with the first appearing only about 10 years ago in 2017. But what is the social significance of Doodles, and why does queer representation in Doodles matter?

Source: Alexander Grey/Pexels

The Social Significance of Google Doodles

With Google holding over 90 percent of the search market share, it is safe to say that nearly all internet users view Doodles on a regular basis (Davies, 2024). Even so, the social significance of Doodles remains largely unexplored. This is surprising because the construction of Doodles is built from the Doodle principles to “educate users by humanizing the search engine through artistic storytelling” (The Story and Evolution of Doodles, Google Doodles, n.d.). The educational focus of Doodles is also dedicated to inclusivity, equality, and cultural diversity in efforts to teach users about historical figures, scientific achievements, or cultural events/holidays they might not otherwise know about while also demonstrating innovation and Google's commitment to technological experimentation through animation, interactivity, and design (Gesenhues, 2016). Due to their everyday presence and social significance, Doodles are ripe for inquiry.

The Current Universe of Queer Doodles

Source: Queer Doodles (2017 to 2026)/Meredith Worthen

Using Google Doodle library’s search engine (Search Our Doodle Library Collection, Google Doodles, n.d.), I located a total of 28 LGBTQ-related content Doodles by searching the following keywords: LGBTQ, lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, pride, rainbow, LGB, and activism. The first queer Doodle was launched on the 66th birthday of Pride Flag creator Gilbert Baker (June 2, 2017). From 2017 to 2020, only one to two queer Doodles appeared per year. In 2021 to 2023, this number was significantly larger, with five to seven queer Doodles per year, but there was only one queer Doodle in 2024 and 2025, and one (thus far) in 2026. Half (n = 14, 50 percent) commemorate birthdays of significant queer persons of interest (e.g., Lili Elbe). A queer flag (e.g., rainbow Pride flag, trans flag) is visible on about half (n = 12, 43 percent) of queer Doodles (e.g., Celebrating Marsha P. Johnson). Many (n = 12, 43 percent) launched during US Pride Month (June) (e.g., Celebrating 50 Years of Pride). See all 28 queer Doodles from 2017 to 2026 here.

The Potential Transformative Power of Queer Doodles

Doodles have been found to have a significant impact on collective memory making (Britten, 2020), global cultural policy (Karaarslan, 2019), and multimodal storytelling (Belova, 2021). Doodles featuring LGBTQ-related content may also be a powerful mechanism to both align with Doodle’s principles of education, inclusivity, equality, and cultural diversity, as well as bring awareness to key queer people and historical events. This is especially important because research shows that engagement with positive queer-related content is related to resilience and positive impacts on the mental health of LGBTQ+ youth (Craig, 2014). Queer Doodles may also introduce a new audience to queer content they might otherwise learn about. Queer media exposure has even been found to reduce discrimination and prejudice toward LGBTQ+ people (Dias et al., 2023).

Source: LExie Blessing/Pexels

More Queer Doodles, Please!

With only 28 existing queer Doodles and the number of annual queer Doodles plummeting in recent years, we need more queer Doodles! Why? Queer Doodles can offer points of education and activism and validate queer existence. In a time when LGBTQ people are experiencing heightened forms of daily discrimination, harassment, and violence (Worthen, 2020, 2024), queer Doodles can be a fun and simple way to remind even a casual Googler that LGBTQ representation matters. Queer Doodles can also help engage with queer activism and other forms of media-related literacy and social justice.

Next time you open up the Google search engine, take a second to check out the Doodle. Some are even hyperlinked to Google short videos, like this one: Celebrating Willi Ninja: Godfather of Voguing. You might learn something new!

item.title: Can a Near-Death Experience Seem to Last for Years?
item.description:
Near-Death Experiences

Can a Near-Death Experience Seem to Last for Years?

Time distortion research explains how the brain creates heaven-like experiences.

Posted August 11, 2026

Key points
  • Multiple studies have demonstrated the brain can significantly slow or speed subjective time flow.
  • Evolutionary, environmental, physiological, and psychological factors dictate our subjective pace of time.
  • The experience of death creates multiple conditions conducive to the subjective slowing of time.
How long can a near-death experience seem to last?
Source: Alejandro De Roa/Pexels

Have you ever had a dream that seemed to last for hours, only to wake up and realize that mere seconds have passed? This is just one example demonstrating the widely accepted neurological understanding that our experience of time is simply a construct of the brain (e.g., Macar et al., 2002; Teghil et al., 2024).

Similarly, many people who have had a near-death experience (NDE) report that it seemed to last far longer than the duration of time their body was recorded as being non-responsive (e.g., Cramer, 2021). Some have claimed a subjective experience lasting years, or even decades (e.g., International Association for Near-Death Studies, 2016). And although we might be tempted to chalk up such claims to modern factors such as chasing social media clout, similar claims have been documented going back centuries (e.g., Springer, 1898).

Such an abundance of NDE reports exists from people of diverse backgrounds and cultures that it’s widely accepted they are not all just blatant fabrications. Regardless of what is “really” happening, the people reporting these experiences often believe what they are saying. The goal of psychology, then, is not to prove these claims objectively wrong, but to explore the subjective experience. And much of that experience comes down to how the brain constructs our perception of time.

How Evolution and Lifespan Influence Time Perception

Under different evolutionary conditions, intelligent beings could easily evolve to experience time much slower or much faster than we do. So why do we experience time at its apparent pace? Maybe it’s related to our lifespan. An organism that lives only 24 hours might experience each second as if it were a day. Conversely, for a being that lives for millennia, a year for us might feel like a day for them. This is supported by studies that show that time perception shifts the older we get (Stojić et al., 2023; Amanatski, 2025).

Or maybe our experienced pace of time flow is, for some reason, a survival advantage related to some external objective rate of change. This could be the chemical processes happening in our environment or even perhaps the speed of light as far as that may limit electrical transmission times between parts of the brain. External factors such as temperature have indeed been shown to alter time perception (Wearden & Penton-Voak, 1995).

Since it’s well-established that the brain creates our experience of time, what is the next step in scientific inquiry? A historical example may help: Before black holes were actually observed, they were hypothesized by asking the question of how far existing models and observations of the theory of relativity could be stretched. Could gravity be so extreme that even light could not escape? The idea seemed ridiculous. There was no observable evidence of this at the time. It was just a question of theoretical limits. But it turns out the answer was yes. I’d like to extend the same scientific inquiry to time distortion.

Theoretical Limits of Time Perception in Near-Death and Dream States

Whatever the case for our usual experience of time, the dream and NDE examples above make clear that the brain controls the throttle. So this raises an interesting theoretical question: What are the limits of the brain’s powers to warp our experience of time relative to the outside world? Could a dream that feels like an hour take place in a minute? A second? Less? What if it could take place in an amount of time that was so close to zero that it might as well be instantaneous?

Now, what if that instantaneous dream didn’t just feel like an hour, but a day? A year? An eternity?

That may sound impossible, but only from a very human-centric and artificially constructed view of what time is. Often, scientists are the first to fall into such a trap. I once had a professor who said that we could not be living in a simulation because the processor parts necessary for that would exceed the number of elementary particles in the universe. What he failed to take into account is that the universe we observe, if it is a simulation, may be much, much smaller than the “real” universe where the hardware is (if it even operated under the same laws of physics).

So at the instant of death, could the brain generate what we might experience as an eternal existence? Intense emotions such as awe have been shown to slow our perception of time (Mella et al., 2019; Rudd et al., 2012; Droit-Volet, 2007). So have factors such as novelty (Yuan et al., 2008), focus (Matthews & Meck, 2016), and altered states of consciousness (Glicksohn & Berkovich Ohana, 2017). It’s hard to imagine an event that could trigger more of these time-distorting factors than death. So it’s possible within the framework of modern neuroscience to hypothesize that our brain may be capable of generating a long-term conscious experience at the moment of death. Only further research will tell.
